items.title: Outstanding Code of Conduct Complaint
items.text:
To consider the report of the Monitoring Officer (copy
enclosed).
Minutes:
The Committee considered the report of the Monitoring
Officer seeking Members’ consideration of how to progress an
outstanding complaint made against a Councillor.
Members were reminded that the Committee at its meeting on
28 April 2026 had considered a report from the Monitoring Officer
(attached as Appendix 1 to the report) and resolved “that the
outstanding complaint made against a Councillor (as set out in the
report) be placed on hold for a further six months (until October
2026) and further information from the Councillor be requested by
the Monitoring Officer”. Since that meeting, further
information had been requested and Appendix 2 detailed the
information received.
Appendix 1 to the report provided details of complaints
received in March 2024 in relation to the behaviour of a Councillor, advised that an
independent investigation had been carried out and noted that
Appendix A to Appendix 1 set out the report arising from the
investigation.
The Director of Legal and Governance introduced the report
and provided the Committee with background information, including
the options available for Members to consider.
In response to a question
regarding Option C which would place the complaint on hold for a
further six months and therefore until after the District Elections
in May 2027, the Director explained that a shorter period could be
selected.
Councillor S J N Morgan proposed that Option A to take no
further action and close the complaint be agreed. This proposal was
not seconded.
Councillor A M Lay referred to the effect the complaint may
have had on other Members and Officers and, taking into
consideration the Nolan Principles, proposed that Option B to refer
the matter to the Joint Standards Committee for a formal decision
be agreed. This proposal was duly seconded.
During the debate that followed, some Members of the
Committee expressed their views regarding the complaint. In
addition, Mr Mitchell, the Independent
Person, provided the Committee with his views. Consideration was
given to the complaint received, the person to whom the complaint
related and the effect on other related parties. In response, the
Director of Legal and Governance explained the options that could
be considered should Members agree Option B.
The Chairperson then put the recommendation to agree Option
B, as proposed by Councillor Lay, to the vote. Upon a vote being
taken, this was duly agreed.
RESOLVED that the Councillor (as set out in the report) who was the
subject of the complaint be given an opportunity to respond to the
draft report and that the matter be referred to the Joint Standards
Committee for a formal decision.

BUDGET MONITORING REPORT – QUARTER 2

1. PURPOSE OF THE REPORT

1.1 To provide Members of the Committee with an updated Quarter 2 (Q2) financial
 position for the Council for the period ended 30 September 2026. Covering the first
 half of the year, this report provides a good indication of the likely outturn and
 identifies a firm basis to support planning for the coming year.

1.2 This matter is brought forward for consideration with the agreement of the
 Chairperson of this Committee to provide assurance that the financial management
 of the council is effective and ensure the sustainability of council operations now and
 into the future.


2. RECOMMENDATIONS

 (i) That Members comment on the forecast revenue outturn as at 30 September
 2026 which is £126,000 over budget (0.9%) and the analysis of this;

 (ii) That Members confirm the change in treatment of Planning Appeal costs;

 (iii) That Members agree the adjustments recommended arising from previous
 Committee decisions for one-off funding now the actual values are known and
 adjustments can be made;

 (iv) That Members consider the forecast capital outturn as at 30 September 2026,

 on this;

 (v) That Members accept the balances held as Earmarked Reserves and
 General balances;

 (vi) That the revenue budget reconciliation be noted.

3.1 Overview

3.1.1 This is a positive report which provides details of the current financial position of the
 council and the expected position at the end of the financial year. All key measures
 are performing within expectations – revenue spending is close to budget, as is
 capital spending, debt is being reduced and reserves continue to be at a good level.



 Our Vision: Where Quality of Life Matters

[page 2]

REPORT of
DIRECTOR OF NEIGHBOURHOOD SERVICES AND COMMUNITIES
to
STRATEGY AND RESOURCES COMMITTEE
26 NOVEMBER 2026

LONG LEASE AGREEMENT: FORESHORES AT RIVER BLACKWATER AND DOWNS
ROAD BOATYARD

1. PURPOSE OF THE REPORT

1.1 To request agreement for a renewal lease of 25 years for the foreshore abutting
 Downs Recreation Ground at River Blackwater.

1.2 To request agreement for a renewal lease of 25 years for the foreshore adjoining
 Downs Road Boatyard to bring both leases in line with each other.


2. RECOMMENDATION

 That the Council agrees a renewal lease for 25 years for the foreshore abutting
 Downs Recreation Ground at River Blackwater and the foreshore at Downs Road
 Boatyard allowing both leases to expire in 2051.


3. SUMMARY OF KEY ISSUES

3.1 The current tenant is a long-standing tenant of Maldon District Council. The
 leaseholder runs a business from the adjoining boatyard using both leased
 foreshores as necessary access points.

3.2 The current tenant has held a lease for the abutting Downs Recreation Ground at
 River Blackwater (see APPENDIX 1 – image A) with Maldon District Council since
 1993. The lease was initially granted for a period of seven years and then extended
 to 25 years.

3.3 The tenant has leased the foreshore area adjoining Downs Road Boatyard
 (APPENDIX 1 - image B) since 2008 under a separate 20-year lease. As this lease
 is nearing the end of its term, approval is sought to extend the lease period to align
 them.

3.4 The lease for the foreshore adjoining Downs Road Boatyard has expired; however,
 the tenant remains in lawful occupation under the security of tenure provisions of the
 Landlord and Tenant Act 1954. This enables the tenant to continue occupying the
 premises on the existing lease terms while a renewal lease is negotiated and
 completed.

3.5 As the security of tenure provisions of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954 were not
 excluded from either lease, the current tenant, has statutory rights to seek a renewal
 tenancy. In practice, this means that the Council is required to grant a new lease on
 broadly similar terms, unless there are statutory grounds for opposing renewal.


 Our Vision: Where Quality of Life Matte

[page 2]
3.6 The Council is therefore working with the tenant to agree new lease terms for both
 the foreshore abutting Downs Recreation Ground on the River Blackwater and the
 foreshore adjoining Downs Road Boatyard. As the additional foreshore lease was
 granted in 2008 for a term of 20 years, it is proposed that the renewal arrangements
 align the terms of both leases.


4. CONCLUSION

4.1 The current tenant has a legal right a new lease on similar terms for the foreshore
 abutting Downs Recreation Ground at River Blackwater and foreshore adjoining
 Downs Road Boatyard under the provisions of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954.
 The proposed 25-year lease will meet our legal obligations and ensure stability for
 the business.


5. IMPACT ON PRIORITIES AS SET OUT IN THE CORPORATE PLAN 2025 - 2028

5.1 Growing our economy

5.1.1 The agreement of a new lease and lease extension will provide stability for the long
 running business, allowing continued investment in the skills and facilities required to
 contribute to Maldon’s maritime heritage.


6. IMPLICATIONS

 (i) Impact on Customers – None.

 (ii) Impact on Equalities – None.

 (iii) Impact on Risk (including Fraud implications) – If Members do not
 approve the proposed lease renewal, the tenant has the right to seek renewal
 of the tenancy by applying to Court. The Court will likely grant a new lease
 and will set the terms, rent etc over which the Council will have less control.

 (iv) Impact on Resources (financial) – There will be no impact on the Council’s
 Finances, as a result of agreeing these lease extensions.

 (v) Impact on Resources (human) – The legal work will be carried out in house.

 (vi) Impact on Devolution / Local Government Reorganisation – None
 currently.

Background Papers: None.

Enquiries to: Jon Sharkey, Director of Neighbourhood Services and Communities.

REPORT of
DIRECTOR OF NEIGHBOURHOOD SERVICES AND COMMUNITIES
to
STRATEGY AND RESOURCES COMMITTEE
26 NOVEMBER 2026

ASSET DISPOSAL POLICY

1. PURPOSE OF THE REPORT

1.1 To consider and approve the Council’s Asset Disposal Policy, attached at
 APPENDIX 1 to this report.


2. RECOMMENDATION

 That the Council’s Asset Disposal Policy attached at APPENDIX 1 to this report be
 approved.


3. SUMMARY OF KEY ISSUES

3.1 The Assets Disposal Policy, attached at APPENDIX 1, establishes a consistent and
 transparent framework for assessing and progressing the disposal of Council-owned
 land and property.

3.2 The Policy identifies three principal disposal routes: open market disposal, disposal
 to special purchasers and Community Asset Transfer. Proposals will be assessed
 against the Council’s operational and strategic requirements, supported by
 appropriate valuation, legal and financial advice. Community Asset Transfer
 applicants will need to demonstrate measurable public benefit, community support,
 financial sustainability and suitable governance, operational and management
 capacity.

3.3 The Policy sets out a staged process covering initial assessment, due diligence,
 options appraisal, independent valuation, engagement, approval and legal
 completion, together with post-completion monitoring and updates to Council
 records.

3.4 Decisions remain subject to the Constitution and Scheme of Delegation. Any decision
 for a large site disposal either by sale or lease will still require Council approval. This
 policy ensures a consistent approach to all requests and ensures Officers have a
 clear policy to follow when making delegated decisions for disposals currently set out
 within the constitution.

3.5 Appropriate safeguards, including restrictive covenants, overage, clawback and
 reversionary provisions, will be considered to protect the Council’s interests where
 appropriate.

3.6 Applicants or purchasers will normally meet the Council’s legal and reasonable
 professional costs unless otherwise agreed in writing.


 Our Vision: Where Quality of Life Matters

[page 2]
3.7 Disposals will not normally be progressed where an asset remains required for
 Council purposes, a substantially similar request has been determined within the
 preceding six months, or an application fails to meet the relevant criteria.

4. CONCLUSION

4.1 Approval of the Assets Disposal Policy will provide a clear governance process for
 the public and officers dealing with requests to purchase Council assets,

5. IMPACT ON PRIORITIES AS SET OUT IN THE CORPORATE PLAN 2025 - 2028

5.1 Delivering Good Quality Services

5.1.1 Having a clear policy will allow the Council to provide clear guidance and
 transparency regarding the management of Council assets. This will allow officers to
 provide a clear process and criteria for assessment of disposal requests.

6. IMPLICATIONS

 (i) Impact on Customers – There are no direct impact on customers arising
 from the recommendations in this report.

 (ii) Impact on Equalities – There are no direct equality implications arising from
 the recommendations in this report.

 (iii) Impact on Risk (including fraud implications) – The Policy ensures that all
 decisions are made in a clear and consistent matter reducing the risk of
 challenge.

 (iv) Impact on Resources (financial) – There are no direct financial implications
 arising from approval of the Policy. Any decisions made will have an impact
 on Council finances, but these will be advised in any future disposal reports.

 (v) Impact on Resources (human) – None.

 (vi) Impact on Devolution / Local Government Reorganisation – There are no
 direct implications arising from the recommendations in this report.


Background Papers:
APPENDIX 1 – Asset Disposal Policy
APPENDIX 2 – Asset Disposal Policy Flowchart

Enquiries to: Frank Britt, Principal Assets Manager

1. Introduction

1.1. Application ref 25/00381/OUTM was first considered at the 5 August District Planning
 Committee. A Member made a motion to refuse the application, but this was not
 seconded and a motion to defer the item was passed, to allow Officers to consider
 the robustness of the potential reasons for refusal and give an opportunity for the
 applicant to provide further information on several concerns raised by the planning
 committee. This Addendum Report will highlight these matters.

1.2. Following the deferral of this application (5 August 2026), an updated version of the
 National Planning Policy Framework (the NPPF) was published (17 August 2026).
 The core direction of the NPPF remains largely unchanged; however, the structure of
 the NPPF has been overhauled, in addition to the presumption in favour of
 sustainable development being changed. An updated report considered by the
 District Planning Committee on the 28 October 2026, provided an assessment in
 regard to the latest version of the NPPF.

1.3. The update report (above) following consideration was subsequently deferr

Matters Raised at the 28th October Committee

1.4. The following matters were raised by members at the 28 October Planning
 Committee, or within an email which officers subsequently received from a member
 requesting legal clarification of several matters.

 Anglian Water Capacity

1.5. The Update Report to the 28 October Committee (hereafter referred to as the ‘update
 report’) provided the following update in relation to Anglian Water capacity:

 During the 5 August committee, Members questioned whether there is sufficient
 capacity in the local sewer system to accommodate the additional flows from the
 multiple live applications in Tollesbury. Officers re-consulted Anglian Water, who
 subsequently advised that the Tollesbury Water Recycling Centre (WRC) has
 sufficient capacity to accommodate c. 639 additional dwellings and that it therefore
 has more than enough capacity for the additional wastewater flows from the
 proposal, the other relevant Tollesbury developments (refs 25/00207/OUTM,
 25/01057/OUTM, 26/00066/OUTM and 26/00161/OUTM). Officers are satisfied that
 there is sufficient drainage infrastructure to accommodate the proposal in a worst
 case scenario, if the live applications in Tollesbury were to be fully built out to utilise
 current infrastructure.

 At the request of Anglian Water, the committee report included a condition requiring
 the submission of a Strategic Foul Water Strategy, prior to the commencement of
 development. This will ensure that a sustainable point of connection to the drainage
 network can be established.

1.6. The legal opinion notes that Anglian Water’s headroom figure for wastewater
 treatment capacity (which equates to c. 639 dwellings) was stated excluding “sites
 with existing planning consent yet to connect to our network”. The five developments
 which were considered within the cumulative assessment amount to 558 homes,
 meaning that Anglian Water are advising there is additional wastewater treatment
 capacity that can accommodate the foul drainage needs arising from this
 development. The catchment for the Tolle

 in terms of the Lund High Court decision. It should be noted that detailed engineering
 drawings are not required with an outline planning application and Anglian Water, as
 the utility operator, are not requiring them to be provided, instead such information
 would be required, if necessary, through the submission of a future application to
 discharge condition 27, which is the usual practice for outline planning permissions.

1.11. There is no evidence that the requirements of the condition have no reasonable
 prospect of being discharged, in particular noting that the condition was requested by

1.12. It should also be noted that foul drainage condition has been secured through other
 planning permissions and appeal decisions across the District. To depart from the
 condition approach and refuse planning permission would go against the consistent
 decision approach that has been taken elsewhere in the District and would expose
 the Council to potential risks in the event that the application was refused planning
 permission and then subject to a planning appeal process. An Inspector would look
 at the approach taken with those recent applications and other appeal decisions in
 the District in their decision making and they would be highly likely to use a planning
 condition to require a foul drainage strategy to be approved.

1.13. The legal opinion notes the question in relation to surface water drainage and
 advises that approving a surface water strategy at outline stage, with the outfall
 consents to be secured later, would not be unlawful nor contrary to national policy on
 sustainable drainage. The requirement in this regard is that there is adequate

 supported by the Lead Local Flood Authority who require through a planning
 condition (Condition 23) to secure a surface water drainage strategy.

 “As set out already, it is a scientific question for the competent authority based on the

 that the Council cannot rule out, even taking into account there is a Grampian
 condition, then the development cannot pass an appropriate assessment. If,
 however, the Council concludes any risk can be ruled out through an appropriate
 Grampian then the appropriate assessment can be passed.

 In circumstances where Essex County Council (ECC) and other bodies consider a
 Grampian can rule out harm, if the Council is taking a different view it will need to
 explain very clearly where the potential problem arises, what the pathway is to harm
 of the protected site, and why that cannot be managed by (for example) condition.

 Similarly, if the Council considers that it is missing information again it will need to
 explain very clearly why it needs that information to make its decision, in light of other
 management measures. So, for example, it would not be enough to simply say that
 no SPOC has been identified where a suitably worded Grampian would delay
 development until one is identified. If the concern is impact on the sewerage system
 itself, the Council will need to consider (a) whether and why a Grampian is not
 sufficient to solve this and (b) the Sewerage Undertaker’s statutory duties in light of
 both the legal position (a rebuttable presumption assuming they will operate
 effectively) and the policy position in DM7 of the new NPPF.”

1.19. The Appropriate Assessment acknowledges the potential significant effects which
 may result from the increased foul flows from the development. The previous section
 of this update report establishes that the Grampian condition is sound and meets the
 legal tests to be used as a suitably worded planning condition that would mitigate the
 harm from the impact of the 

[page 6]
That said it is not for the developer to have to fix pre-existing issues. So again that
 might indicate a Grampian might be the appropriate solution rather than (for
 example) requiring the developer to go further.”

1.21. The LPA is not in receipt or knowledge of any clear evidence that Anglian Water are
 directly failing in their duty to protect the adjacent designated nature conservation
 sites in any way which relates to the current application. Officers do not consider this
 to be a reason for refusal and the recommended foul water strategy Grampian
 condition can effectively mitigate the proposed development’s impacts.

 Primary School Education Contribution

1.22. ECC Education have supported the application subject to a financial contribution
 towards a primary school transport. While the NPPF does not consider the use of
 private motor vehicles to be sustainable, the school transport method is not a private
 motor vehicle trip.

1.23. The updated legal opinion goes on to consider the implications of this mitigation on
 the sustainability of the Site, as was raised by a member in email following the 28
 October committee. The opinion sets out that NPPF Policy TR3 test is whether
 development limits the need to travel “particularly by private car” and whether it offers
 a “genuine choice of transport modes for residents and users”. This is not a
 requirement that every journey, or all primary school journeys has to be made on foot
 or by bus. While a safe and connected pedestrian route is the preferred approach,
 the development would be acceptable in light of the proposed mitigation through the
 school bus service and appropriate weight should be given to this consideration, as
 part of the wider application. It, as stated, remains the choice of the individuals to
 walk to the primary school or use the bus service. Officers maintain that the Site is
 well-related to Tollesbury and is a sustainable location within the context of the
 NPPF.
